blocks.text: A 62-year-old man can walk about 200 metres before a cramping pain grips his calf; within a few minutes of standing still it fades. Imaging shows his femoral artery is narrowed. Why should a narrowing that looks modest on a scan starve the muscle of blood so badly? The answer lies in how flow, pressure and resistance are related.

blocks.markdown: Blood moves through the circulation for the same reason water moves through a pipe: there is a **pressure difference** between the two ends. Flow does not depend on the absolute pressure at one point, only on the pressure drop along the path, and on how hard the path is to flow through. That 'hardness' is called **resistance**. Every vessel, every organ and the whole circulation can be described with just these three quantities: flow (Q), pressure difference (ΔP) and resistance (R).

blocks.title: Flow, pressure difference and resistance
blocks.text: Flow (Q) is the volume of blood passing a point per unit time, measured in mL/min or L/min. Pressure difference (ΔP) is the inlet pressure minus the outlet pressure, in mmHg. Resistance (R) is the opposition to flow offered by the vessels; it is defined by R = ΔP / Q, so its unit is mmHg per (L/min). Resistance cannot be measured directly in life; it is calculated from ΔP and Q.

blocks.caption: The circulatory form of Ohm's law: flow rises with the pressure difference and falls with resistance.

blocks.title: Total peripheral resistance of the whole circulation
blocks.prompt: A resting adult has a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 93 mmHg, a right atrial pressure of 3 mmHg and a cardiac output of 5 L/min. Calculate the total peripheral resistance (TPR).

steps.text: The whole systemic circulation runs from the aorta (inlet, mean pressure MAP) to the right atrium (outlet), so the pressure difference is MAP minus right atrial pressure.
The flow through the whole systemic circulation is the cardiac output, 5 L/min. Rearrange Q = ΔP / R to R = ΔP / Q.

blocks.answer: TPR = 18 mmHg per (L/min). Note that the right atrial pressure is so small that it is often ignored, which would give about 19; the answer depends on the stated outlet pressure.

blocks.markdown: What sets the resistance of a single vessel? The French physician Poiseuille showed that, for **steady, laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a long, rigid, straight cylindrical tube**, resistance depends on three things: the length of the tube (L), the viscosity of the fluid (η) and the radius of the tube (r). Longer tubes and thicker fluids resist more; wider tubes resist less. Blood is not a perfect Newtonian fluid and vessels are neither rigid nor perfectly straight, so the equation is an excellent guide to direction and approximate size rather than an exact prediction.

blocks.caption: Poiseuille's law for resistance: η is viscosity (Pa·s), L is vessel length (m), r is internal radius (m).

blocks.title: Radius to the fourth power
blocks.text: Because resistance varies as 1/r^4, small changes in radius cause very large changes in resistance and flow. Halve the radius and resistance rises 16-fold; double the radius and resistance falls to one sixteenth. Length and viscosity matter only in proportion (a doubling gives a doubling), so in the body, changes in radius are by far the most powerful way of altering regional flow.

blocks.title: A 20 per cent narrowing of an artery
blocks.prompt: An artery supplies a tissue at a fixed pressure difference. Atheroma reduces its internal radius by 20 per cent. By what factor does resistance increase, and what happens to flow? Assume length and viscosity are unchanged.

steps.text: The new radius is 0.8 times the old radius, so r_new = 0.8 r_old.
Resistance varies as 1/r^4, so the ratio of new to old resistance is 1 divided by 0.8 raised to the fourth power.
At constant pressure difference, flow is inversely proportional to resistance, so flow falls to 0.4096 of its original value, that is to about 41 per cent.

blocks.answer: Resistance rises about 2.4-fold and flow falls to about 41 per cent of normal: a one-fifth narrowing of the radius removes roughly 59 per cent of the flow.

blocks.caption: Pressure and compliance along the circulation. Values are typical approximations and vary between individuals and texts.

blocks.markdown: **Compliance** describes how much a vessel stretches when the pressure inside it rises. A highly compliant vessel accepts a large extra volume for a small pressure rise. Veins are far more compliant than arteries, which is why the veins act as a **blood reservoir**: they hold most of the blood volume, and constricting them squeezes blood back towards the heart. Arteries, by contrast, are stiff enough to hold pressure but elastic enough to smooth the pulses from the heart.

blocks.caption: Compliance C: the change in volume held (mL) per unit change in distending pressure (mmHg).

items: Vessels in series (for example artery, arteriole, capillary, venule, vein along one path): resistances add, so the total is larger than any single one.
Vessels in parallel (for example the separate organ beds branching from the aorta): the reciprocals add, 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ..., so the total is smaller than the smallest single resistance.
Adding another parallel bed therefore lowers total peripheral resistance, while constricting arterioles in many beds raises it.
Higher viscosity (for example a high haematocrit) raises resistance in proportion; anaemia lowers it.

blocks.title: Do not confuse pressure with resistance
blocks.text: A vessel can carry a high pressure and offer low resistance (the aorta), or carry a low pressure and a very high resistance (a contracted arteriole). The arterioles, not the capillaries, produce the biggest pressure fall because their muscular walls allow radius, and hence resistance, to change so dramatically.

points: Flow equals the pressure difference divided by resistance: Q = ΔP / R, and total peripheral resistance equals (MAP minus right atrial pressure) divided by cardiac output.
Poiseuille's law gives R proportional to ηL / r^4 for laminar flow in a rigid tube, so radius dominates: halving radius raises resistance 16-fold.
Arterioles are the main resistance vessels; veins are the highly compliant capacitance vessels holding most of the blood volume; capillaries are low-pressure exchange vessels.
Resistances add in series and their reciprocals add in parallel, which is why the organs, arranged in parallel, together offer a low total peripheral resistance.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between flow (Q), pressure difference (ΔP) and resistance (R) in a vascular bed?

options.text: Flow equals the pressure difference between inlet and outlet divided by resistance
Flow equals the inlet pressure multiplied by resistance
Flow equals resistance divided by the pressure difference
Flow is determined by the absolute inlet pressure alone, whatever the outlet pressure

questions.correctOptionText: Flow equals the pressure difference between inlet and outlet divided by resistance

distractorRationale.b: Multiplying by resistance would make flow rise as the path became harder to traverse, the opposite of reality.
distractorRationale.c: This inverts the relationship; flow would fall as the driving pressure difference rose.
distractorRationale.d: It is the difference between the two ends, not the absolute value at one end, that drives flow.

questions.explanation: Flow through any vessel or organ is driven by the pressure difference across it and opposed by resistance, so Q = ΔP / R. Doubling the pressure difference doubles flow, whereas doubling resistance halves it.

questions.stem: A patient has a mean arterial pressure of 100 mmHg, a right atrial pressure of 4 mmHg and a cardiac output of 4.8 L/min. Calculate the total peripheral resistance in mmHg per (L/min).
questions.explanation: The pressure difference across the systemic circulation is MAP minus right atrial pressure, 100 - 4 = 96 mmHg. Dividing by the flow (cardiac output) gives R = 96 / 4.8 = 20 mmHg per (L/min).

questions.stem: An arteriole constricts so that its internal radius falls to half its original value. Assuming vessel length and blood viscosity are unchanged, what happens to the resistance of that arteriole?

options.text: It doubles
It increases 4-fold
It increases 8-fold
It increases 16-fold

distractorRationale.a: This treats resistance as inversely proportional to radius rather than to radius to the fourth power.
distractorRationale.b: This uses radius squared, which is the dependence of cross-sectional area, not of resistance.
distractorRationale.c: This uses radius cubed, which does not appear in Poiseuille's law.

questions.explanation: Poiseuille's law gives resistance proportional to 1/r^4. With r halved, the new resistance is 1 / (0.5)^4 = 16 times the original, which is why modest arteriolar constriction has such powerful effects on flow.

questions.stem: A segment of a coronary artery supplying a region of myocardium is narrowed by plaque so that its internal radius is reduced by 30 per cent. The pressure difference across the segment, the length and the blood viscosity all remain constant. By what percentage does flow through the segment fall? Give your answer in per cent.
questions.explanation: The new radius is 0.7 of the original, and flow at constant pressure difference is proportional to r^4, so the new flow is (0.7)^4 = 0.2401 of the original, about 24 per cent. The fall in flow is therefore 100 - 24 = 76 per cent.

questions.stem: At rest, which part of the systemic circulation contains the largest fraction of the total blood volume?

options.text: Large systemic arteries
Arterioles
Systemic veins and venules
Systemic capillaries

distractorRationale.a: Arteries are high pressure but hold only a small fraction of the blood because their walls are stiff.
distractorRationale.b: Arterioles are resistance vessels with a very small total volume.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the highly compliant veins and venules hold roughly 60 to 65 per cent of the blood volume.
distractorRationale.d: Capillaries are numerous but their total volume is small, only a few per cent of the total.

questions.explanation: Veins and venules are thin-walled and very compliant, so they accommodate a large volume at low pressure and are called capacitance vessels. This is why venous constriction can shift blood centrally to the heart.

questions.stem: The same increase in distending pressure is applied to a segment of artery and to a segment of vein of identical length and initial volume. The vein accepts a much larger added volume. What property best explains this?

options.text: The vein has higher resistance
The vein has higher compliance
The vein has a higher viscosity of blood
The vein has a higher mean intraluminal pressure

distractorRationale.a: Resistance describes opposition to flow, not the volume a vessel stores for a given pressure rise.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: compliance is the volume change per unit pressure change, C = ΔV/ΔP, and it is far greater in veins.
distractorRationale.c: Viscosity is a property of blood, not of the vessel type, and does not set storage capacity.
distractorRationale.d: Venous pressure is actually lower than arterial pressure; the question concerns the same applied pressure rise.

questions.explanation: Compliance is defined as the change in volume per unit change in pressure. For the same pressure rise, the more compliant vein accepts a much greater volume, which is why veins serve as the blood reservoir.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a long-standing lung disease develops secondary polycythaemia, with the haematocrit rising from 0.45 to 0.65. Assume vessel length and radius are unchanged. What is the most likely effect on the resistance to blood flow in his vessels?

options.text: Resistance decreases because there are more red cells carrying oxygen
Resistance is unchanged because only vessel radius determines resistance
Resistance increases because blood viscosity rises
Resistance decreases because blood becomes more compliant

questions.correctOptionText: Resistance increases because blood viscosity rises

distractorRationale.a: Oxygen-carrying capacity does not enter the resistance equation; viscosity does.
distractorRationale.b: Radius is the dominant determinant but viscosity enters directly, with resistance proportional to η.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: a higher haematocrit raises blood viscosity and, with it, resistance in proportion.
distractorRationale.d: Compliance is a property of the vessel wall, not of the blood, and does not decrease resistance.

questions.explanation: Poiseuille's law makes resistance directly proportional to viscosity, and viscosity of blood rises steeply as haematocrit increases because red cells interact and impede shear. Radius and length are stated to be constant, so the higher viscosity raises resistance.

questions.stem: Two organ beds are supplied in parallel from the same arterial pressure and drain to the same venous pressure. Bed X has a resistance of 12 mmHg per (L/min) and bed Y has a resistance of 4 mmHg per (L/min). Calculate the combined resistance of the two beds in mmHg per (L/min).
questions.explanation: For parallel resistances the reciprocals add: 1/R = 1/12 + 1/4 = 1/12 + 3/12 = 4/12 = 1/3, so R = 3 mmHg per (L/min). The combined value is less than the smaller individual resistance, which is why the whole body's total peripheral resistance is low even though each vascular bed is individually resistive.

questions.stem: A narrowing halves the internal radius of a segment of a long artery. Using Poiseuille's law, explain quantitatively what happens to resistance and to flow if the pressure difference is unchanged, and state two assumptions on which the law depends.
markingGuide: States Poiseuille's law: resistance is proportional to viscosity times length divided by radius to the fourth power
Calculates that halving radius raises resistance 16-fold
Uses Q = ΔP / R to deduce that flow falls to one sixteenth (about 6 per cent) of its original value at constant pressure difference
States that small changes in radius therefore have disproportionately large effects on flow
Names two assumptions, for example steady laminar flow, Newtonian fluid, long straight rigid tube, constant viscosity
Optionally notes that real vessels and blood only approximate these assumptions, so the result is a guide to direction and approximate size
questions.explanation: Resistance is proportional to 1/r^4, so halving r multiplies resistance by 2^4 = 16 and, at constant pressure difference, flow falls to 1/16 of its original value. The law holds for steady laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid in a long, straight, rigid tube, which real arteries and blood only approximate.

questions.stem: Compare arteries, capillaries and veins in terms of their typical pressures and compliance, and explain how each feature suits the function of that vessel type.
markingGuide: Arteries: high, pulsatile pressure (mean about 90 mmHg) and low compliance, suited to conducting blood and maintaining driving pressure; elastic recoil smooths flow between beats
Capillaries: low pressure (about 35 falling to about 15 mmHg) and thin walls, suited to exchange rather than storage
Veins: very low pressure and very high compliance, so they act as capacitance vessels holding most of the blood volume
States that venous compliance is many times that of arteries, or that veins hold about 60 to 65 per cent of the volume
Links venous constriction to redistributing blood centrally, or links arteriolar resistance to the pressure fall before the capillaries
questions.explanation: Pressure falls progressively along the circulation, with the steepest drop across the arterioles, so capillaries receive blood at a pressure low enough to avoid damage but high enough to drive exchange. Veins combine low pressure with high compliance, letting them serve as a reservoir that can be mobilised by venoconstriction.
